name: LSQUIC (LiteSpeed QUIC)
workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8GB file over a 10Gbit/s link between two dedicated bare-metal hosts, using an extended QUIC Interop Runner; all client/server pairs across 6 QUIC libraries measured, 50 repetitions per pair.
claimed_speedup: LSQUIC-LSQUIC pair: 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche pair: 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x, derived from page data, Fig. 3); with 32x larger UDP receive buffers and architecture-tuned compile flags, LSQUIC*-LSQUIC*: 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche*-quiche*: 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x, derived from page data, Fig. 10)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the baseline pairs (example/default builds of each project were used); optimized variants (LSQUIC*/quiche*) used unspecified 'compile flags to optimize for the used architecture' (exact flags not given in the paper text extracted)
hardware: Default: AMD EPYC 7543 (32-core), Broadcom BCM57416 NIC, Debian Bullseye, kernel 5.10.0-8-amd64. Also repeated on AMD EPYC 7551P, Intel Xeon D-1518, Intel Xeon E5-1650, Intel Xeon Gold 6312U (paper Table I).
tradeoffs: Goodput is highly asymmetric by client/server combination: in this same study the quiche-server/LSQUIC-client pair reaches more than 2x the goodput of the LSQUIC-server/quiche-client pair, so the 'LSQUIC beats quiche' result holds for matched same-vendor pairs, not universally across mixed pairs. LSQUIC showed unintended retransmission behavior with BBR congestion control in this study (paper forced Cubic/Reno for all libraries to keep the comparison fair).
caveats: Peer-reviewed (IFIP Networking 2023 / EPIQ lineage, ISBN 978-3-903176-57-7) and the measurement framework + configs + results are published (github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper, confirmed the CPU table matches the paper), but the paper text itself does not state the compiler or exact compile flags for the baseline (non-optimized) pairs, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A.
found_via: arXiv API search_query=all:QUIC AND all:implementation AND all:performance -> arxiv.org/abs/2309.16395 'QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links'

name: LSQUIC-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)

claimed_speedup: LSQUIC-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaged 11019 Mbit/s vs MsQuic-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaging 8118 Mbit/s (~1.36x); also beats quiche-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaging 6168 Mbit/s (~1.79x) in the same table (derived from page data)
hardware: Bare-metal server pair; NIC using the Intel 'ice' driver (E810 family) with SR-IOV. Exact CPU model not found in the repository content inspected this session.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: Same DPDK/SR-IOV deployment complexity as other entries in this family (dedicated NIC/queue, hugepages, root). A separate table in the same dataset (measurement-data/01-implementation-matrix/processed.csv) shows msquic-dpdk NOT beating vanilla kernel msquic (7982 vs 8250 Mbit/s), so DPDK's benefit is very implementation-dependent; only the head-to-head DPDK-vs-DPDK cross-library comparison used here is a clean win for LSQUIC-DPDK.
caveats: Same unpublished-paper caveat as the quiche-DPDK entry above (DOI TODO, NOMS 2026); numbers come straight from the group's published CSV rather than paper prose. Treat the ratio as directional given some inconsistency between the two published data tables for msquic-dpdk.
found_via: Same discovery path as quiche-DPDK entry: gh api orgs/tumi8/repos -> tumi8/quic-bypass-paper -> measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv

name: Nail (NailDNS demo server)
workload: Authoritative-DNS-server load test: random zone file (50,000 domains) and random query sequence with 10% NXDOMAIN, run for one minute against a Nail-generated DNS server and against BIND 9.5.5 on the same local machine.
claimed_speedup: median throughput ~139,215 qps (NailDNS) vs ~47,234 qps (BIND 9.5.5), approximately 3x faster; median per-query latency 0.139 ms vs 0.416 ms (derived from page data, box-plot figure)
tradeoffs: NailDNS is a 295-line research demo built to showcase the Nail parser-combinator toolkit (grammar-driven parsing/generation with dependent fields and stream transforms); it implements only zone parsing, query answering, and label compression, none of BIND's dynamic reconfiguration, TSIG, notify, or DNSSEC-signing machinery. Not a drop-in BIND replacement.
caveats: Peer-reviewed OSDI'14 paper (USENIX) with raw box-plot data embedded in the LaTeX source, but no CPU model or compiler/flags are stated anywhere in the paper or repo, capping the tier at B. Benchmark is against BIND 9.5.5, a release from 2009; project has been unmaintained since 2020. Set usability to 'reference' since the demo server is a minimal example, not intended as a production DNS library.
found_via: GitHub code search: 'times faster than BIND' -> jbangert/nail paper/login/eval.tex and paper/osdi14/performance.tex

name: ngtcp2
workload: quicperf: an apples-to-apples C++ benchmark harness running the same shared TLS material, saturation policy, and socket backend (syscall/io_uring) against native adapters for ngtcp2, LSQUIC, TQUIC, quiche, picoquic, XQUIC and several Rust/Zig stacks, over loopback UDP with CUBIC congestion control. Scenarios include bulk download/upload, bidirectional transfer, multistream transfer, loss recovery, and flow-control-limited transfer.
claimed_speedup: ~1.6-2.1x quiche on bulk-transfer scenarios (p50, syscall backend, derived from page data): download 18.227 vs 11.258 Gbps, upload 31.047 vs 14.794 Gbps, bidirectional 20.503 vs 12.662 Gbps, multistream upload 24.816 vs 15.291 Gbps, loss-recovery 17.379 vs 11.689 Gbps, flow-control 15.600 vs 10.309 Gbps
compiler_and_flags: quicperf C++ harness: Release build, -O3, native CPU flags, LTO by default (per README); quiche's Rust packet engine built via quicperf depofile with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3", CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1
tradeoffs: C library requiring an external TLS backend (OpenSSL/BoringSSL/GnuTLS/wolfSSL/picotls) and manual event-loop integration, unlike quiche's more batteries-included Rust API. In the same quicperf harness ngtcp2 is markedly slower than quiche and most peers on connection-establishment rate (113 vs 277 conn/s, syscall) and on plain request/response rate (51,386 vs 64,574 rps), so its measured advantage is specific to sustained bulk-transfer throughput, not connection setup or small-request rate.
caveats: quicperf's committed run-environment file (docs/results/fixed-full-matrix-max16-20260601T175816Z/fixed-environment.txt) records only an anonymized machine_hash, with no CPU model, so hardware is not stated -- this caps the entry at Tier B despite public benchmark code and documented build flags. Benchmark is loopback-only (not a physical/WAN link). Several ngtcp2 rows in this table are flagged 'inconclusive' (tripped a CI/spread/drift gate) rather than 'publishable', though ngtcp2's lead over quiche held in both the inconclusive and publishable rows across syscall and io_uring backends.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "ngtcp2" "benchmark" -> victorstewart/quicperf; numbers read directly from docs/latest-results.md and docs/methodology.md

name: picoquic
workload: quicperf loopback harness: QUIC client-to-server bulk Upload scenario, CUBIC congestion control, syscall UDP backend, 2 client threads, both rows publishable status.
claimed_speedup: 15.823 Gbps p50 (picoquic) vs 14.794 Gbps p50 (quiche) on the Upload scenario, ~7% faster (derived from page data); also 297 vs 277 connections/second p50 on the Connect scenario, ~7% faster (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: quicperf CMake Release build: -O3, native CPU flags, LTO by default; exact compiler/version not published
tradeoffs: picoquic is a minimal, largely single-threaded reference/research QUIC stack. It only leads quiche on 2 of 16 quicperf scenarios (Upload throughput, Connect rate); quiche wins the other 14, often by a wide margin (e.g. request/response 64,574 vs 59,098 qps, stream churn 74,756 vs 48,480 streams/s), so this is workload-specific, not general superiority.
caveats: quicperf (victorstewart/quicperf) is an independent third-party multi-stack QUIC benchmark harness, not picoquic's or quiche's own benchmark. CPU model is not published in the harness's README, methodology.md, or results doc, so the entry is capped at tier B despite public benchmark code and stated build flags. Both compared rows carry the harness's own 'publishable' (passed audit gates) status.
found_via: GitHub: victorstewart/quicperf docs/latest-results.md, Upload and Connect scenario tables (orchestrator-flagged quicperf harness)

name: quic-zig
workload: quicperf loopback harness: QUIC Connect scenario (full handshake + first stream creation), CUBIC congestion control, syscall UDP backend, 8 client threads, both rows publishable status.
claimed_speedup: 286 connections/second p50 (quic-zig) vs 277 connections/second p50 (quiche), ~3% faster (derived from page data)

name: QUICHE (Google)
baseline: TCP+TLS (HTTPS over TCP, pre-QUIC production stack)
workload: Live production A/B experiment across billions of Chrome, YouTube app, and Google Search app users comparing Google's QUIC implementation (predecessor of this repo, now called QUICHE) against HTTPS-over-TCP for search page latency and video rebuffer rate
claimed_speedup: 8.0% Google Search latency reduction for desktop users and 3.6% for mobile users; 18.0% YouTube rebuffer-rate reduction for desktop users and 15.3% for mobile users (paper Section on 'Application Performance')
stars_or_usage: ~900 stars; powers Chromium, Envoy proxy, and Google's production servers (>30% of Google's egress traffic over QUIC per the paper)
tradeoffs: UDP-based transport needs OS/kernel support (GSO/GRO) for high throughput and historically costs more CPU per byte than TCP; large dependency footprint (BoringSSL, Abseil); embedding API is designed for Google-scale integrators (Chromium/Envoy), not a drop-in small library.
caveats: The cited numbers are from the SIGCOMM 2017 paper 'The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment', measured on Google's original gQUIC implementation (the ancestor of today's IETF-QUIC code in this repo), not a controlled lab benchmark against any of this task's named baselines (c-ares/quiche/msquic/nghttp3) directly, and no compiler/hardware details are given since it is a live production measurement, not a lab benchmark. Google's C++ 'QUICHE' should not be confused with Cloudflare's Rust 'quiche' (one of this task's baselines) or Cloudflare's separate 'quiche' repo -- they are unrelated, same-named projects. README text ('actively developed and maintained', 7,655 commits) confirms active status but an exact last-commit timestamp could not be retrieved this session due to a shared GitHub API rate limit.
found_via: GitHub code search for 'quic' in vcpkg.json/README files turned up Cloudflare's quiche and litespeedtech/liblsquic; cross-checking the QUIC ecosystem for C++ implementations not already catalogued surfaced google/quiche (used by Chromium/Envoy), then the SIGCOMM 2017 deployment paper was located via research.google's publication page linked from the project.

name: TQUIC
workload: quicperf: same shared C++ harness as the ngtcp2 entry above, measuring fresh-stream HTTP-style request/response rate, stream churn (open/send/receive/finish), tiny-message rate, and 0-RTT request/response under a 16-client-thread saturation scout, over loopback UDP.
claimed_speedup: ~2.1-2.4x quiche on request/message-rate scenarios (p50, syscall backend, derived from page data): request/response 155,043 vs 64,574 rps, stream churn 178,272 vs 74,756 streams/s, small-payload messages 176,604 vs 73,852 msgs/s, 0-RTT request/response 154,448 vs 65,327 rps
compiler_and_flags: TQUIC built via quicperf depofile with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3", CARGO_BUILD env BORINGSSL_LIB_DIR set, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1; C++ harness built -O3/native CPU flags/LTO by default
tradeoffs: Implemented in Rust (exposes C/C++ FFI, not a native C++ library). In the same harness TQUIC loses to quiche on raw bulk download throughput (8.6-8.9 vs 9.8-11.3 Gbps) and on resumed-connection rate (216 vs 306 conn/s, syscall), so its measured edge is specific to request/response and stream-churn rate, not bulk transfer.
caveats: Same anonymized-hardware limitation as the ngtcp2 entry above (no CPU model recorded in quicperf's committed environment file) caps this at Tier B. TQUIC also publishes its own first-party benchmark (https://tquic.net/docs/further_readings/benchmark) claiming to be 'four to five times faster' than Google's QUICHE-G and 'up to 20%' faster than LSQUIC on an AMD EPYC 7K62 testbed, but that page gives only chart images (no raw numbers or benchmark source) and compares against QUICHE-G/nginx-quic/LSQUIC rather than Cloudflare's quiche directly -- first-party only, so on its own it would rate Tier C; it is not used as the primary evidence here.

name: ls-qpack
baseline: nghttp3 (QPACK encoder compression ratio); nghttp2/nginx Huffman coder (shared HPACK/QPACK Huffman alphabet)
workload: Huffman encode/decode of real HTTP header samples (short header, Facebook x-fb-debug header, paragraph-length text) run 1e5-1e9 iterations (litespeedtech/benchmarks repo); separately, QPACK compression ratio (compressed bytes / QIF source bytes) on a captured Facebook response header trace, compared directly against nghttp3's QPACK encoder.
claimed_speedup: Huffman decoder 1.15-1.96x faster than nginx's decoder; Huffman encoder 2.37-5.77x faster than nghttp2's encoder (also 1.11-2.12x vs nginx, 1.18-3.59x vs h2o); QPACK compression ratio 0.16-0.18 vs nghttp3's 0.21-0.39 (lower=better) on a Facebook response header trace (derived from page data: roughly 1.3-2.2x more compact).
stars_or_usage: 86 stars; used in OpenLiteSpeed, LiteSpeed Web Server and Web ADC
tradeoffs: Vanilla C99 with a lower-level API (struct lsxpack_header); needs wrapping for higher-level languages (Go/Python/Rust/TS/Ruby wrappers exist but are separately maintained third-party projects).
caveats: The 2019 Huffman timing posts compare against nginx's and nghttp2's Huffman coder, not nghttp3 directly, and state no compiler flags or CPU model, which caps the timing claim at tier C. The 2021 QPACK-ratio post does name nghttp3 directly but measures compression ratio (bytes on the wire), not runtime speed, and is a first-party, non-replicated comparison.
found_via: Blogs: seed query 'QUIC performance benchmark blog' led to h2o/quicly and other QUIC libs; ls-qpack README links to blog.litespeedtech.com/2019/10/03/fast-huffman-encoder/, /2019/09/16/fast-huffman-decoder/, and /2021/04/05/qpack-mnemonic-technique/, all opened directly.

name: Caladan
baseline: Parties (authors' reimplementation, 'Parties*', because the original source was unavailable); also compared with Linux (kernel TCP, BE task at SCHED_IDLE) and Shenango
workload: memcached 1.5.6 (Facebook USR mix, ~1 us service time) at 800,000 requests/s over TCP, colocated with swaptions-GC (a PARSEC job using the Boehm GC); 99.9th-percentile latency measured over 20 ms windows during a 120 s run. A second test colocated memcached with the stream-DRAM bandwidth antagonist and compared against Linux and Shenango (Fig. 4).
claimed_speedup: 99.9% latency 11,000x lower than Parties* during GC cycles ('reducing tail latency from 580 ms to 52 us'), and BE throughput about 5% higher than Parties*. Against Linux and Shenango (constant stream-DRAM interference, Fig. 4): their tail latency rose 'up to 235x and 6x higher than without interference' and Shenango's throughput fell 75%, while Caladan kept similar tail latency with and without interference and 'much higher throughput than Linux and Shenango' (no exact numbers, graph only). KSCHED vs a variant using Linux syscalls (sched_setaffinity/tgkill/eventfd): the Linux variant needs 43x more scheduling work and 5x the scheduling latency when moving 22 tasks, and tops out at ~285,000 core reallocations/s vs Caladan's peak of 560,000.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The current repo build (build/shared.mk) uses CC ?= gcc with -O3 -DNDEBUG (plus optional -march=native -flto -ffast-math when CONFIG_OPTIMIZE is set), -std=gnu11. These are today's flags, not the 2020 evaluation build.
hardware: Server with two 12-core (24-hyperthread) Intel Xeon Broadwell CPUs (exact model not stated) and 64 GB RAM, running Ubuntu 18.04 with kernel 5.2.0 modified for faster multicast IPIs (Linux baseline on kernel 5.4.0). Only socket 0 used; 40 Gb/s Mellanox ConnectX-5 NIC; 280 GB Intel Optane NVMe. Clients were quad-core machines with 10 Gb/s ConnectX-3 NICs behind a Mellanox SX1024 switch. TurboBoost, C-states, frequency scaling and THP were off, as were the Meltdown/MDS mitigations. Caladan ran with 22 guaranteed LC cores plus one physical core for the scheduler.
stars_or_usage: 200 stars, 78 forks. Per the paper, it is derived from Shenango's open-source release (a new scheduler plus the ksched module).
tradeoffs: Apps must link Caladan's own runtime (green threads, its own TCP/UDP stack) and are not Linux-compatible. A pthread shim runs PARSEC-style batch jobs unmodified, but network services have to be ported, and LC tasks must expose concurrency with a thread per connection or per request (the authors changed memcached this way). It takes one dedicated scheduler core (iokerneld, run as root), the ksched kernel module and hugepages. It runs best with its own mlx5 driver on ConnectX-4 or newer; DPDK PMDs work but are slower, and directpath needs Mellanox OFED, DEVX firmware and root. It is x86-64 Linux only, cannot manage interference across NUMA nodes, and its hyperthread co-scheduling does nothing about transient-execution attacks between sibling hyperthreads.
caveats: The 11,000x figure is against the authors' own reimplementation of Parties, which they gave kernel-bypass networking and hyperthreads (hence 'Parties*'). It is a peak-window value taken only during GC cycles (580 ms vs 52 us), not a steady-state average; the separate 500,000x figure is convergence speed compared with Parties' published typical speed. The Linux and Shenango comparison exists only as a graph (Fig. 4): the 235x and 6x ratios compare those systems with and without interference, not with Caladan, and Caladan's throughput lead over Linux comes mostly from kernel-bypass networking. The Linux baseline also ran a different kernel (5.4.0 vs modified 5.2.0). IX and Arachne appear in related work only and were not measured. No compiler or flags are given, and the CPU is named only as 'Xeon Broadwell'; security mitigations were disabled. The artifact repo (github.com/shenango/caladan-all, which has no license file) has scripts for the Caladan-only figures and the ksched-vs-pinned run, but none for the Parties*, Linux/Shenango (Fig. 4) or Linux-syscall-variant comparisons. These are 2020 numbers, and the code has changed a lot since then (current kernels 5.15/6.8, directpath, DPDK PMDs).

name: eRPC
baseline: conventional kernel TCP/UDP socket-based RPC (and specialized RDMA-only systems like FaSST/HERD)

hardware: Mellanox CX3-CX5 or DPDK-capable NICs (exact CPU model not stated on the pages opened this session; full details are in the NSDI'19 paper PDF, which could not be text-extracted via WebFetch)
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs and huge pages; a binary RPC library, not an HTTP-semantics server (no TLS/HTTP parsing); app must integrate its session/event-loop model
caveats: NSDI'19 paper's own baseline is conventional TCP/UDP RPC and other specialized RDMA systems, not nginx/Boost.Beast/actix-web/uvloop directly, so baseline_in_list=false; exact hardware CPU model and compiler flags could not be confirmed from the pages opened (WebFetch could not extract readable text from the PDF); category fit is RPC-over-network rather than literal HTTP serving, included because the assignment's own starting query explicitly targets kernel-bypass high-performance server research. Authors now point new users to a successor project, microsoft/machnet, for DPDK-based messaging (checked; 162 stars, MIT, active, but its README states only an absolute number '750K RPS at 61us P99.9' with no named baseline comparison, so it does not itself qualify under rule 1).

name: epoll-httpd

name: ChaChaCha
baseline: OpenSSL ChaCha20/ChaCha20-Poly1305 (assembly and EVP), BoringSSL stitched AVX2 ChaCha20-Poly1305
workload: ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD seal/open at protocol-realistic sizes (QUIC 1200-1350B, WireGuard 1360-1420B, 4KB TLS record, 9000B jumbo, 16384B TLS 1.3 max record, 32-64KiB bulk) measured in core cycles/byte via perf_event_open, pinned to one core, best-of-7 internal reps x best-of-3 runs, on AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
claimed_speedup: AEAD seal vs OpenSSL: +19.3% to +47.6% across sizes on Zen5 (e.g. +45.4% at WireGuard 1360-1420B, +22.4% at 16384B); vs BoringSSL: +49.4% to +57.4%; vs Intel IPsec-MB: +3.8% to +19.9%. Raw AVX-512 ChaCha20 vs OpenSSL: +25-33% on Zen5, +5-8% on Zen4 for >=4KB streams. Raw AVX2 ChaCha20 vs OpenSSL and BoringSSL: +10% Zen5, +7-8% Zen4 for messages above a few KB
compiler_and_flags: gcc, CFLAGS=-O2 -Wall, ASFLAGS=-Wa,--noexecstack (NASM/perlasm for kernels)
hardware: AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5, Turin) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2/AVX-512 only (no portable/scalar-only fallback path shown as competitive); OpenSSL is measured both as raw vendored assembly (openssl-asm) and via EVP (openssl-evp) which carries provider dispatch overhead, so the EVP-vs-EVP comparison would show an even larger margin than the asm-vs-asm numbers quoted; BoringSSL comparison for AVX-512 is AEAD-only since BoringSSL has no AVX-512 ChaCha20 raw kernel; single author, very new/unreviewed project
caveats: Single-author project with only 1 GitHub star and no independent review; author explicitly documents methodology carefully (per-call fixed-overhead table) and shows all four implementations round-trip-checked for correctness, which is unusually rigorous for a solo project, but numbers have not been reproduced by anyone else

name: curve25519 (mehdi sotoodeh / "Mehdi")
baseline: OpenSSL Ed25519 (EVP_PKEY_ED25519 via the EVP API), OpenSSL 1.1.1
workload: Ed25519 key-pair creation, public-key derivation, X25519 shared-secret computation, and Ed25519 message signing, timed in CPU cycles via TSC read, comparing this library's hand-written x86-64 assembly implementation ('make asm && make openssl') against OpenSSL's EVP_PKEY_ED25519 API for the same operations
claimed_speedup: On HP EliteBook 755 G5 (Ubuntu 18.04.2, OpenSSL 1.1.1): CreateKeyPair 64.50% faster (74,822 vs 210,738 cycles), CreateSharedKey 38.81% faster (270,930 vs 442,750 cycles), SignMessage 81.53% faster (78,628 vs 425,656 cycles); but CalculatePublicKey is 51.45% SLOWER than OpenSSL (316,096 vs 208,714 cycles). Separately, standalone X25519 base-point scalar multiplication is claimed 6.2x-19.5x faster than Google's curve25519-donna (not OpenSSL) across several platforms/compilers, fastest at 43,229 cycles on an Intel Core i7-2670QM
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ via 'make asm' (hand-written x86-64 assembly kernels, not affected by the portable-C build's missing -O level); portable-C fallback build uses CFLAGS=-DNDEBUG -m64 -Wno-format with no explicit -O2/-O3 (Release build sets only -DNDEBUG per Rules.mk), but this does not affect the asm path that is actually benchmarked against OpenSSL
hardware: HP EliteBook 755 G5, x86_64 (OpenSSL comparison); Intel Core i7-2670QM (internal cycle-count tables); exact CPU model for the OpenSSL comparison run not given beyond laptop model
tradeoffs: One of four benchmarked operations (CalculatePublicKey) is markedly slower than OpenSSL, so the library is not a strict win across the board; portable-C build has no stated optimization level (only the asm build is used for the OpenSSL comparison); constant-time/blinding variants are slower than the non-hardened V1.1 numbers; abandoned since 2020, predates OpenSSL 3.x and modern OpenSSL X25519/Ed25519 assembly optimizations, so the OpenSSL side of the comparison is likely stale
caveats: Benchmark is from 2015-2019 era against OpenSSL 1.1.1 on a single laptop; OpenSSL has significantly optimized its X25519/Ed25519 assembly since 1.1.1, so the margin may have shrunk or reversed on current OpenSSL; the curve25519-donna comparison (6.2x-19.5x) is a different, non-KNOWN_LIST baseline and mixes results across different compilers/platforms rather than one apples-to-apples run

name: EverCrypt (HACL*) Curve25519 (Vale-optimized)
workload: Curve25519 scalar multiplication (the ECDH key exchange used in TLS 1.3), cycle count per operation, measured with a Linux kernel crypto benchmarking suite
claimed_speedup: EverCrypt's targeted (Vale-assembly) Curve25519 implementation narrowly exceeds OpenSSL's by ~3% (also ~1% faster than Oliveira et al.'s hand-written asm and ~22% faster than Erbsen et al./fiat-crypto's verified C)
benchmark_url: https://project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf (Figure 9, 'EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider', IEEE S&P 2020)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.3, -O3 -march=native -mtune=native
hardware: Intel Kaby Lake i7-7560U
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; EverCrypt/HACL* code is used in Firefox NSS and other Project Everest artifacts
tradeoffs: Source is written in F*/Low*/Vale and compiled via KaRaMeL to C/assembly rather than hand-written C; gains formal proofs of memory safety, functional correctness and secret-independence (constant-time) at the cost of a heavy build toolchain (F*, KaRaMeL, Vale) compared to a plain C/asm library.
caveats: The paper's headline claim is mostly 'matches or exceeds' OpenSSL rather than a large win — the concrete beat documented with full methodology is only ~3% on this one primitive (Curve25519) on one 2017-era CPU. The same paper's AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305 figures (Figs. 7-8, i9-9900K) show EverCrypt's targeted implementation roughly matching OpenSSL's rather than clearly beating it, so do not extrapolate the 3% figure to other primitives. The actively-maintained home for production use has since moved to https://github.com/cryspen/hacl-packages.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: HACL* GitHub README citation trail to the EverCrypt IEEE S&P'20 paper PDF (project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf), located after arXiv queries for 'verified cryptographic OpenSSL performance' surfaced only related/adjacent papers

name: rustls
workload: TLS 1.2/1.3 full handshake and resumed handshake rate, bulk AES128-GCM send/receive throughput, and per-session memory footprint; rustls 0.22.0 (aws-lc crypto provider) vs OpenSSL 3.2.0, from the aochagavia/rustls-bench-results 2023 ISRG-funded benchmark.
claimed_speedup: TLS1.2 full handshake (client): 4,992 vs 2,581 handshakes/sec (1.93x); resumed handshakes 80-330% more per second; AES128-GCM send 6,712 vs 6,504 MB/s (1.03x) but receive 6,018 vs 7,234 MB/s (0.83x, slower); ~13KiB vs ~69KiB memory per session, 131.8MB vs 688.4MB for 10,000 concurrent sessions (-81%); ChaCha20-Poly1305 throughput ~45% slower than OpenSSL

caveats: Numbers were read from the bencher.dev case-study summary of the aochagavia/rustls-bench-results dashboard (2023 run) plus a 2019 jbp.io post; exact compiler flags are not fully itemized. rustls is itself one of the three named incumbent baselines for this category (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, rustls), so this entry documents rustls's own standing vs OpenSSL rather than a third-party project beating rustls.

name: ztls
workload: Sans-I/O TLS 1.3 in-memory application-data round trips (client-to-server, server-to-client, ping-pong) at record sizes 16B, 128B, 1350B, 8192B, 16384B, across TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, over caller-owned in-memory transport (no sockets), n=10 captures with formal confidence intervals

name: Machnet
baseline: Linux kernel TCP/IP stack (sockperf with Nagle disabled for microbenchmarks; kernel-TCP builds of a FASTER KV server and of Hashicorp Raft's transport)
workload: Round-trip latency of 64 B echo messages between two Azure F8s_v2 VMs in the same availability zone, one message in flight (Fig. 10). Also a single-threaded FASTER KV server doing 100% GETs over 100M 8-byte keys (Fig. 6), and Hashicorp's Go Raft replicating 80 B commands across 3 VMs (Fig. 8).
claimed_speedup: 'Linux TCP's latency is 2.6x, 4.2x, and 7.4x higher than Machnet at median, p99, and p99.9' (64 B echo; Machnet median 27 us). FASTER KV: '3.3x higher throughput, with 700K RPS compared to Linux TCP's 210K RPS', and at 210K RPS a p99 of 50 us vs 250 us (80% lower), using 2 cores vs 100% of all 8 for Linux. Go Raft: 34% lower median latency and 37% lower p99 (p50 185 us vs 282 us, p99 625 us vs 1000 us).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo's src/CMakeLists.txt Release build uses C++20 with -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions and needs DPDK 23.11. The Docker image builds on Ubuntu 22.04 with build-essential; no compiler version is pinned.
hardware: Azure F8s_v2 VMs (8 vCPUs, 16 GB DRAM) with accelerated networking, Ubuntu 22.04.2, Linux kernel 6.2, same region and availability zone, no proximity placement groups. Hugepages and pinned stack processes for the DPDK stacks; no isolcpus or IRQ steering. The CPU model is not stated. The repo's PERFORMANCE_REPORT lists the Azure F8s_v2 vNIC as CX4-Lx with the netvsc PMD.
stars_or_usage: 162 stars, 33 forks. The task lead says the eRPC authors point new users to it.
tradeoffs: Machnet runs as a separate busy-polling sidecar that takes at least one dedicated engine core. It needs a second, dedicated vNIC per VM that is unbound from the kernel, plus DPDK and hugepages; the prebuilt image comes from GHCR and needs a GitHub token. Apps use its own sockets-like shared-memory message API (machnet_attach/listen/connect/send/recv), not BSD sockets, so they must be ported (C shim with Go, Rust and JS bindings). Its reliable, connection-oriented message protocol only talks to other Machnet peers, so it cannot replace TCP for outside clients. In exchange it runs on basic cloud vNICs (Azure, AWS, GCP) without flow steering, and it supports multiple processes per NIC and blocking receives. Each shared-memory crossing costs ~250 ns, and new connections are handled on a 50 us periodic interval.
caveats: The numbers come from arXiv v1 (Feb 2025, 'Fast Userspace Networking for the Rest of Us', where the figures still label the system 'CNet'). That is a pre-review, first-party version. The peer-reviewed paper is 'Enabling Fast Networking in the Public Cloud', ASPLOS '26, pp. 679-696, with a changed author list (confirmed via Crossref, Semantic Scholar and PoliMi IRIS). Its full text could not be read because ACM DL returned 403 and IRIS has no file, so the final numbers are unverified. That is why this is tier C; it would be B if the ASPLOS text keeps these comparisons. The Linux baseline is untuned: Nagle is off, but busy-polling sockets, isolcpus and IRQ steering are not mentioned, while Machnet dedicates a polling core. Against eRPC (a listed baseline) Machnet is slower: its median and p99 are within 10% of eRPC and p99.9 within 23%, and its 27 us median is 2 us higher. gRPC was not measured; the paper only asserts that libraries on top of Linux TCP such as gRPC would be slower. Only one Azure region was used, and the paper says cross-cloud numbers are not comparable. On the repo side, only msg_gen is in the tree; the FASTER server and Raft port were not found, and the Linux side used sockperf. The README headline (750K 1KB RPCs/s at 61 us P99.9) has no baseline.
